name: read-tree-discards-your-edit
description: git read-tree HEAD to fix a shared-index deletion guard silently reverts your unstaged working file — stage first, re-seed second
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

`git read-tree HEAD` is the fix the ledger wrapper *recommends* when a shared
index trips its deletion guard. It also **overwrites unstaged working-tree
files** from HEAD. If your edit is on disk but not yet staged, running it to
"clean up the index" destroys the edit, and the commit that follows reports
`no changes added to commit` — which reads like a no-op, not like data loss.

Case (AJCR, 2026-07-29, review-ajcr run 0082 s0006). Ten lanes share one ledger
index. My commit hit `ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_DELETIONS`; the wrapper's own advice is
`git read-tree HEAD && git add -- <your files> && git commit`. I ran it, and the
50-line board retraction I had just written to `AJCR.w4-rep.yaml` was gone —
disk equal to HEAD, `grep -c` for my headline returning 0 on both. I had to
regenerate the whole edit from context. Earlier in the same session the same
sequence worked, because there I happened to write, stage, *then* hit the guard.

**Why:** this is not the hazard already recorded in
[[explicit-paths-dont-protect-shared-index]] or
[[commit-with-pathspec-not-index]] — those are about committing *too much*
(another lane's staged snapshot riding along). This one loses *your own* work,
and the failure signature is the opposite: a clean-looking "nothing to commit".
Because the recommended remedy causes it, the instinct to trust the tool's own
hint is what does the damage.

**How to apply:** when the guard fires, stage your file **first**, then re-seed:
`git add -- <your files>` before `read-tree`, or re-seed and immediately re-apply
the edit. Cheapest reliable check afterwards, before assuming a commit was a
no-op: `grep -c '<a distinctive phrase from your edit>'` on the file and on
`git show HEAD:<path>`. If disk says 0, the edit is gone — regenerate it rather
than re-running the commit.

Prefer writing board edits with a script that is **idempotent and re-runnable**
(mine asserted the marker was absent before prepending), so recovering from this
is a re-run rather than a reconstruction. Related:
[[verify-board-at-head-not-worktree]] — same discipline, and the same
`git show HEAD:` check catches both.

`pic0RepresentableByOfCharts` (`Picard/Pic0SigmaSheaf.lean:161`) has three antecedents, and
the board tracks them on three separate rows: `IsChartUniv` (c9b), Zariski-local surjectivity

three compose — discharge each and the seam fires.

**They do not compose as stated.**  The atlas the seam consumes is a family of *restricted*
charts `restrictChart (abelSigmaChart …) (V i)` (`Picard/Pic0ChartAtlasParamFree.lean:86`),
whose source is `(V i : Scheme)` — an open of the *chart source*, i.e. of the divisor scheme.
So the coverage antecedent, unfolded through `chartsCoverLocally_of_pointwise`
(`Pic0ChartCoveragePointwise.lean:128`), must produce a chart point
`x : (W : Scheme) ⟶ (V i : Scheme)` landing **in that same `V i`**, while coverage geometry
produces a point of the divisor scheme `D.left` with no such constraint.  The two opens the
route wants to identify live on different objects — `V i` on the divisor scheme, `chartLocus`
on the test — and no declaration in the tree relates them.

That is an obligation *between* two antecedents, owned by no row, and it is why "close c9b,
then close B-6" would not have composed even with both closed.

It names the coupling and derives restricted coverage from unrestricted coverage together
with a range containment: the coverage witness, viewed in the chart source, factors
set-theoretically through `V i`.  Given that, the witness lifts to `V i` along the open
immersion `(V i).ι` by `IsOpenImmersion.lift`, and the class it names is unchanged because
`restrictChart` is *by definition* precomposition with `yoneda.map (V i).ι` — so the lift's
chart value is the unlifted one, with no transport.
